items.title: 4.8 Interconversion of potential energy and kinetic energy

source_refs.note: Topic 4.8 with Figs. 4.12 and 4.13 and Examples 4.5 and 4.6 (PDF 87-89, printed 84-86). The exercise (PDF 89-92) is not reproduced.

blocks.text: Consider a body of mass m at rest at a height h above the surface of the Earth (Fig. 4.12). At position A the body has PE = mgh and KE = 0. We release the body, and as it falls we can examine how the kinetic and potential energies associated with it interchange. At position B, when the body has fallen a distance x (ignoring air friction), PE = mg (h - x) and KE = (1/2) m vB^2. The velocity vB at B follows from vf^2 = vi^2 + 2gS with vf = vB, vi = 0 and S = x: vB^2 = 0 + 2gx = 2gx, therefore KE = (1/2) m (2gx) = mgx. The total energy at position B is PE + KE: total energy = mg (h - x) + mgx = mgh ... (4.19). At position C, just before the body strikes the Earth, PE = 0 and KE = (1/2) m vC^2, where vC^2 = vi^2 + 2gh = 2gh as vi = 0; so KE = (1/2) m vC^2 = (1/2) m x 2gh = mgh. Thus at point C the kinetic energy equals the original value of the potential energy of the body.

blocks.alt: A block of mass m at A, height h above the ground C, falls straight down. Arrows give x from A to B, (h - x) from B to C and h from A to C. Beside them: at A, P.E = mgh and K.E = 0; at B, P.E = mg (h - x) and K.E = mgx; at C, P.E = 0 and K.E = mgh.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.12: A body of mass m falling from height h: P.E and K.E at A, B and C (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.12).

blocks.text: Actually, when a body falls its velocity increases, because it is accelerated by gravity; the increase in velocity increases its kinetic energy. On the other hand, as the body falls its height decreases and hence its potential energy decreases. Thus we see (Fig. 4.13) that loss in PE = gain in KE: mg (h1 - h2) = (1/2) m (v2^2 - v1^2) ... (4.20), where v1 and v2 are the velocities of the body at heights h1 and h2. This result is true only when the frictional force is not considered. If a frictional force f is present during the downward motion, a part of the PE is used in doing work against friction, equal to f h, and the remaining PE = mgh - f h is converted into KE: mgh - f h = (1/2) m v^2, or mgh = (1/2) m v^2 + f h ... (4.21). Thus loss in PE = gain in KE + work done against friction, and conversely loss of KE = gain in PE + work done against friction.

blocks.alt: A falling block of mass m. Its earlier position, drawn dashed, is at height h1 above the ground, where its velocity is v1; at its present position its velocity is v2 and the height of its base is h2.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.13: A falling body with velocity v1 at height h1 and v2 at height h2 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.13).

blocks.title: Example 4.5
blocks.text: A car weighing 1100 kg moves at 12 m s^-1. When it is at point P its engine stops. If the frictional force is 120 N, what is its velocity at point Q (1.5 m higher, 24 m along the road), and how far beyond Q will it go before coming to rest? Solution: the kinetic energy at P is partly converted into PE and partly used up in doing work against friction up to Q, so loss of KE = gain in PE + work against friction: (1/2) m (vi^2 - vf^2) = w h + f d, (1/2) x 1100 kg x (144 m^2 s^-2 - vf^2) = (1100 kg x 9.8 m s^-2 x 1.5 m) + 120 N x 24 m, 550 kg (144 m^2 s^-2 - vf^2) = 16170 kg m^2 s^-2 + 2880 kg m^2 s^-2, (144 m^2 s^-2 - vf^2) = 19050 / 550 = 34.6 m^2 s^-2, vf^2 = 144 - 34.6 = 109.4 m^2 s^-2. Velocity at Q: vf = sqrt(109.4) = 10.5 m s^-1. If the car stops at point R, then (1/2) m v^2 = f S: (1/2) x 1100 kg x 109.4 m^2 s^-2 = 120 kg m s^-2 x S, so S = 501 m approximately.

blocks.alt: A road rises in a straight line from P to Q, 24 m along the slope, while Q is 1.5 m higher than P; from Q the road runs level to R. A dotted horizontal line from P and a double arrow at Q mark the 1.5 m rise.
blocks.caption: Example 4.5 (PDF page 88): the road from P up to Q and on to R (original drawing after the textbook's figure in this example).

blocks.title: Example 4.6
blocks.text: An object of mass 3 kg falls from a height of 15 m and strikes the ground at 16 m s^-1. Calculate the average frictional force of the air. Solution: loss of PE = gain in KE + work done against friction; as vi = 0, w h = (1/2) m v^2 + f h: 3 kg x 9.8 m s^-2 x 15 m = (1/2) x 3 kg x (16 m s^-1)^2 + f x 15 m, 441 kg m^2 s^-2 = 384 kg m^2 s^-2 + 15 m x f, or f = (441 - 384) kg m^2 s^-2 / 15 m = 3.8 kg m s^-2 = 3.8 N.
